catalog_quote: [p.171] Although significant variation pervaded early descriptions of Hadza prosody, Hadza is a tonal language. Hadza contrasts two tone levels—High (á) and Low (à)—with the mora as the tone bearing unit (Coburn et al., forthcoming). Each mora surfaces with a tonal value of H or L. However, some morphemes are underlyingly toneless /∅/ and receive tonal specification via tonal phonological processes, such as tone polarity (see Section 6.3). Contour tones—LH rising and HL falling—only occur on (bimoraic) long vowels, composed of two level tones on separate tone bearing moras. ... new_statements.quote: [p.171] Although significant variation pervaded early descriptions of Hadza prosody, Hadza is a tonal language. Hadza contrasts two tone levels—High (á) and Low (à)—with the mora as the tone bearing unit (Coburn et al., forthcoming). Each mora surfaces with a tonal value of H or L. However, some morphemes are underlyingly toneless /∅/ and receive tonal specification via tonal phonological processes, such as tone polarity (see Section 6.3). [p.158] These vowel lengthening morphemes prompted Sands (2013b:117) to analyze them as causing stress shift. However, this thesis does not find stress in Hadza.

However, some morphemes are underlyingly toneless /∅/ and receive tonal specification via tonal phonological processes, such as tone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hadza is analysed as a two-tone (H/L) language with the mora as tone-bearing unit and all H/L combinations attested on roots of 1-3 moras; the author explicitly finds no word stress (earlier 'stress'/'stress shift' observations are reanalysed as tone plus morphological vowel lengthening). The older instrumental description (Sands, Maddieson & Ladefoged 1996:178) instead called the system unclear and 'best accounted for by analysing Hadza as a pitch accent language, with prominence shifting from one syllable to another according to the context', noting high-toned syllables are longer and more stressed and word melodies LHL / HL.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; Coburn denies stress altogether. (Berger 1943, per Coburn p.167, marked 'stronger' and 'weaker' dynamic accents without analysis.)
new_statements.exceptions: No stress rule, hence no exceptions. Tonal notes: contour tones restricted to bimoraic long vowels; toneless suffixes/enclitics take polar tone; automatic downstep (HLH -> HLM); tonal functional load in roots is low.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (root + affix) tonal analysis from elicited citation and frame forms ('Is a ___' copular frame, imperative verb forms); Sands et al. 1996 explicitly say prominence shifts with context and that interaction with larger prosodic constituents was not worked out.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe Hadza as spoken in the Mang'ola / Lake Eyasi area (Coburn 2024: fieldwork 2022 with speakers from several areas; Sands et al. 1996: Mang'ola consultants). No dialect split is relevant; glottocode hadz1240 applies directly.

sources.note: Ch. 6 (printed pp. 165-190): Hadza is a tonal language, two tones H vs L, mora = TBU, contour tones only on long vowels, toneless suffixes get tone by polarity; printed p. 158: 'this thesis does not find stress in Hadza' (rejecting Sands 2013b:117 stress-shift analysis of vowel-lengthening enclitics); pp. 165-170 review every earlier prosodic statement (Obst 1912 accent marks, Bleek 1931/1939 'variable stress', Berger 1943 dynamic accents, Tucker et al. 1977 tone+stress, de Voogt 1992 primary stress with free variation, Sands et al. 1996 pitch accent, Miller 2011 three tones + stress, Sands 2…

The paper is a working paper on the semantics of masculine/feminine gender assignment in c. 1,400 Hadza nouns (gender/number suffixes -Ø/-ko/-bi'i/-pi'i/-be'e/-pe'e, semantic classes, noun pairings). It has no phonology, prosody, tone or stress section, its transcriptions carry no tone or stress diacritics, and it says nothing about word stress…
